title: The one-lakh car
hook: You built a car for families who squeeze onto one scooter. Now you have to make them want it.
role: You run the Nano project at Tata Motors, 2008 to 2010

profit.label: Profit
profit.hint: The money the Nano makes or loses on each car

future.label: Image
future.hint: How much families trust the Nano and want to be seen in one

intro.text: Years ago, your chairman, Ratan Tata, kept seeing families of four or five on one scooter, often on slippery roads in the dark. Since then, he has wanted to build them a car: safe and cheap enough to own. That car is now your job.

goal.text: It is called the Nano: four seats for ₹1 lakh, before taxes and delivery costs. To reach that price, the basic model has no AC, no radio and no power steering. The plan is to sell 2.5 lakh cars a year, and in a few days the whole world will see it.

d1.title: What will it be known for?
d1.setup: On 10 January you will show the Nano for the first time at the Auto Expo, India's big car show in New Delhi, and every TV channel will be there. It will be the cheapest car in the world, and your sales team says the price will sell it by itself. But the people you built it for have never owned a car.
d1.question: What is the one message you want people to remember?
d1.advisor: A low price gets us into every paper in the world. Nothing else we say will travel that far.

options.label: Show four real seats and very low running costs. Buyers may need time to work out how much they save.
options.outcome: Your ads talk about mileage, low running costs and four real seats. Some buyers ask smart questions about mileage. But at tea stalls people still repeat the price, and they remember 'cheap', not 'good value'.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. Low running costs matter, and you made them clear. But you sold a saving, not the pride of a family's first car.
options.better: Lead with the family and their pride in a first car, then show the low running cost as proof.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you sold the Nano on value. That helps, but buyers also want to feel proud of what they own.

options.label: Make ₹1 lakh the main message: the world's cheapest car. Every paper in the world will print it.
options.outcome: On 10 January 2008 the Nano is shown at the Auto Expo in New Delhi. Tata calls it the People's Car, but the ₹1 lakh price becomes the main story. The press calls it the world's cheapest car, and soon your own people are calling it that too.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. The price got the Nano noticed everywhere, but it also became its name. Nobody wants the neighbours to see them in 'the cheapest car'.
options.better: Sell it as a safe, proud first car for the family, a step up from the scooter. Let the price be a happy surprise.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you made the price the headline. People also buy what a product says about them.

options.label: Show a family moving from a scooter to their first car, and say the price last. Fewer papers may print it.
options.outcome: On the big screen at the Auto Expo, a family steps off a wet scooter and into a Nano. The price appears only at the end. The papers still print ₹1 lakh, but people remember the proud family in its first car.
options.why: Remember: people pay for a result and a feeling. The result was a safe ride, and the feeling was pride in a first car. You sold both, and the price became a happy surprise.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you sold the Nano as a proud first car. People buy a feeling, not just a price.

text.text: In October 2008, after protests over the land for its new plant at Singur, West Bengal, Tata pulls out and moves the Nano plant to Sanand in Gujarat. The launch is delayed. Then, on 23 March 2009, the world's cheapest car is finally launched in Mumbai.

In October 2008, after protests over the land for its new plant at Singur, West Bengal, Tata pulls out and moves the Nano plant to Sanand in Gujarat. The launch is delayed. Then, on 23 March 2009, the Nano is finally launched in Mumbai, and people talk about it as a family's first car.

In October 2008, after protests over the land for its new plant at Singur, West Bengal, Tata pulls out and moves the Nano plant to Sanand in Gujarat. The launch is delayed. Then, on 23 March 2009, the Nano is finally launched in Mumbai.

d2.title: More buyers than cars
d2.setup: Bookings open on 9 April, and you expect a huge rush. But the new Gujarat plant is more than a year away, so until then your old plant at Pantnagar, in Uttarakhand, can make only about 50,000 Nanos a year. Back in 2008, Tata also promised that the first 1,00,000 buyers would pay the launch price.
d2.question: How do you handle the rush?
d2.advisor: Every booking brings cash in today. But every buyer we keep waiting will remember it.

options.label: Close bookings once you have as many as you can build in a year. Many people will miss out for now.
options.outcome: Bookings close within days, and many people are angry that they missed out. But every buyer gets a car within a year, and soon happy owners are showing them off in every town. A second round, at a higher price, waits for the Gujarat plant.
options.why: Remember: a long queue means your price is too low, or you make too little. You could not make more yet, so you kept the queue to what you could build. The new round came later, after the rush and with warning, so your promise held.
options.takeaway: In 2009 you took only the orders you could fill. A promise you can keep beats a crowd you cannot serve.

options.label: Let everyone book, then pick the first 1,00,000 buyers in a fair lucky draw. The others must wait their turn.
options.outcome: In just over two weeks, more than 2 lakh people book a Nano, and nearly ₹2,500 crore comes in. In June a draw picks 1,00,000 buyers, and deliveries begin in July. But a year later, only about 45,000 cars have reached their owners, and some buyers cancel.
options.why: Remember: a long queue means your price is too low, or you make too little. The draw was fair and kept your promise. But 1,00,000 cars from a plant that makes 50,000 a year meant about two years of waiting, and buyers who wait too long start to doubt.
options.better: Take only the orders you can fill soon. Open a new round, at a higher price, when the Gujarat plant is ready.
options.takeaway: In 2009 you took far more orders than you could fill. A long wait turns excited buyers into doubters.

options.label: Raise the price a little before bookings open, so fewer people book and nobody waits long.
options.outcome: The queue is shorter, but the news is about one thing: the Nano no longer costs what you promised. People who trusted that promise feel cheated, and many families who could only just afford the car walk away.
options.why: Remember: raise prices for real costs, never to grab a rush moment. You broke a price you had promised in public, before anyone had even waited. Your costs had not changed; only the crowd had grown.
options.better: Keep the promised price for this round and take only what you can build. Charge more in later rounds.
options.takeaway: In 2009 you broke a price promise to shorten the queue. Lost trust costs more than the money you gain.

text.text: In June 2010 the Gujarat plant opens, built to make 2.5 lakh cars a year, and your second round of bookings starts to fill. But another problem has been growing: the cost of materials like steel and rubber has gone up fast.

In June 2010 the Gujarat plant opens, built to make 2.5 lakh cars a year. The anger over your price rise has faded a little. But another problem has been growing: the cost of materials like steel and rubber has gone up fast.

In June 2010 the Gujarat plant opens, built to make 2.5 lakh cars a year, so at last you can start clearing the queue. But another problem has been growing: the cost of materials like steel and rubber has gone up fast.

d3.title: Costs go up

setup.text: Every Nano now costs more to build. Your chairman promised India a ₹1 lakh car, and the whole country remembers it. The first 1,00,000 buyers were told they would pay the old price, and many are still waiting for their cars.

Every Nano now costs more to build. You have already raised the price once, and buyers have not forgotten. Many who booked at the new price are still waiting for their cars, and your chairman still wants the Nano to stay a car that families can afford.

Every Nano now costs more to build. Your chairman promised India a ₹1 lakh car, and the whole country remembers it. Your first buyers got their cars at the promised price, and the second round was booked at a higher one.

d3.question: What do you do about the price?
d3.advisor: Steel costs more for every carmaker in India. But buyers remember every word we said about ₹1 lakh.

options.label: Keep today's price for everyone, as your chairman once promised, and push suppliers for cheaper parts. Each car will earn less.
options.outcome: Buyers cheer, but even with cheaper parts, each Nano now earns almost nothing. You ask suppliers for lower prices and delay new features. The board starts asking how long you can keep selling your best-known car this way.
options.why: Remember: raise prices to cover real costs, in small steps you tell buyers about first. Keeping your word to early buyers was right. Holding the price for everyone, while costs kept rising, was not.
options.better: Keep today's price for buyers already booked. Raise it for new buyers in small steps, and tell them first.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you held a price your costs could not support. A promise that keeps losing money cannot last.

options.label: Keep today's price for buyers already booked. For new buyers, raise it a little now and a little more a few months later.

outcome.text: In July 2010 the price goes up 3 to 4% for new buyers, because costs have risen sharply. The first 1,00,000 buyers keep the old price, as promised. On 1 November it rises again for new bookings, by about ₹9,000. The one-lakh car is gone.

You raise the price a little for new bookings, then a little more a few months later, while your first buyers keep what they paid. Some people complain, but most understand that steel costs more for everyone.

options.why: Remember: raise prices to cover real costs, in small steps you tell buyers about first. You kept your word to early buyers and passed on real costs bit by bit, with a reason each time.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you kept your promise to early buyers and raised the price for new ones in small steps.

options.label: Raise it once for all new buyers, enough to cover the whole cost, and explain why. Buyers face one rise, not two.
options.outcome: New bookings now cost much more. Your costs are covered, but the papers call it the end of the one-lakh car. Many families who were saving for a Nano give up.
options.why: Remember: raise prices to cover real costs, in small steps you tell buyers about first. Raising the price was fair, because costs had gone up, and you explained why. But one big jump shocked buyers.
options.better: Keep today's price for buyers already booked. Raise it for new buyers in small steps, and tell them first.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you raised the price in one big jump. Small steps keep more buyers with you.

d4.title: Sales fall

setup.text: It is December 2010. Only 509 Nanos were sold in November, the lowest since launch and the fourth fall in a row, far below the 2.5 lakh a year you planned. A few Nanos have caught fire, and buyers find it hard to get loans, while families who want to look rich choose more costly cars over 'the cheapest car'.

It is December 2010. Each Nano still earns almost nothing, and now sales are falling too, because a few Nanos have caught fire and buyers find it hard to get loans. Each month, fewer families walk into the showrooms, and sales are far below the 2.5 lakh a year you planned.

It is December 2010, and sales have fallen month after month, down to a few hundred cars. A few Nanos have caught fire, and buyers find it hard to get loans, while families who want to look rich choose more costly cars over 'the cheapest car'.

It is December 2010. A few Nanos have caught fire, and buyers find it hard to get loans. Most owners still like their cars, but sales have dropped sharply this autumn, far below the 2.5 lakh a year you planned, and each month fewer families walk into the showrooms.

d4.question: How do you win buyers back?
d4.advisor: Unsold cars are filling the dealers' yards, and every month costs us. Whatever we do, it has to work fast.

options.label: Cut the price and offer cheap loans. The showrooms could fill within weeks, though each car earns less.
options.outcome: The showrooms are busy for a few weeks. Then the fires return to the news, and the price cut makes buyers sure of their fear: even Tata thinks the Nano is worth less. Sales sink again, and you have less money than before.
options.why: Remember: a discount doesn't fix a weak product, and it makes a good one look cheap. Buyers were worried about safety and about how the car made them look. A price cut fixed neither, and made the car look even cheaper.
options.better: Fix the real worry first, with a long free warranty and safety upgrades, then keep improving the car.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you cut the price to fix a trust problem. A discount can make a cheap image even worse.

options.label: Stop making the Nano. The losses end, and the Gujarat plant can build bigger cars that earn more.
options.outcome: The plant stays busy, and the losses stop. But families who trusted the Nano feel let down, while rival carmakers win the small-car buyers you leave behind.
options.why: Remember: a discount doesn't fix a weak product, and walking away doesn't fix it either. You stopped the losses before you had tried to fix the real worries, safety and image.
options.better: Find out why buyers stayed away and fix it: a long warranty and safety upgrades, then keep improving the car.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you dropped a product before trying to fix the reasons buyers stayed away.

options.label: Give every Nano a free four-year warranty and safety upgrades. It costs a lot, with no promise that sales will rise.

outcome.text: In December you give every Nano, old and new, a free four-year warranty, on top of the free safety upgrades offered in November. Sales climb again, and the year to March 2012 is the Nano's best ever, at about 75,000 cars. But that is far below the 2.5 lakh a year you planned, and the 'cheapest car' name still sticks.
You give every Nano, old and new, a free four-year warranty and free safety upgrades. It costs you a lot, but worried buyers start coming back, and owners tell their friends the car is safe.

options.why: Remember: a discount doesn't fix a weak product, and it makes a good one look cheap. Buyers were worried about safety, so you fixed that first, at your own cost, and kept the price.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you fixed the real worry, safety, instead of cutting the price.

text.text: Families who once squeezed onto one scooter now drive their Nanos to weddings and work. The Gujarat plant runs close to full, and across India, 'Nano' becomes the word for a family's first car.
You made a few wrong turns, but you kept the families you built it for at the centre. The Nano becomes a car people are proud to park outside their homes, and the Gujarat plant stays busy.

survivor.title: A small car with a small following

text.text: You stop the Nano while some families still love it. The Gujarat plant earns well making bigger cars, but the dream of a car for scooter families ends early. Rivals take the buyers you leave behind.

The price cut brings a short rush, then sales fall again. The Nano lives on with loyal owners who love it, but it never gets the crowds you planned for, and the Gujarat plant never runs anywhere near full.
Your fixes win back many buyers, but the 'cheapest car' tag never fully goes away. The Nano sells steadily for years, though far below the 2.5 lakh a year you planned.
The Nano finds loyal owners who love it, but never the crowds you planned for. It sells steadily for years, while the Gujarat plant never runs anywhere near full.

collapse.title: The car no one wanted to be seen in

text.text: Over the next years the Nano gets power steering, a CNG version and an automatic gearbox. But one relaunch focuses on low monthly payments, making it look even cheaper. In 2013 Ratan Tata calls the 'cheapest car' label a mistake. By 2015 the Gujarat plant runs at about 15% of what it can make, and in 2018 the Nano is stopped.
The price cuts never bring the crowds back. The cars still lose money, the Gujarat plant sits mostly empty, and a few years later the Nano is stopped.
You stop the Nano before its problems are fixed. Rival carmakers win the small-car buyers you leave behind, and the dream of a car for every scooter family ends early.

Your fixes help, but they come too late to win back the crowds. The Nano stays on sale for a few more years while the Gujarat plant sits mostly empty, and the dream of a car for every scooter family slowly fades.
Sales never recover. The Nano stays on sale for a few more years, but the Gujarat plant sits mostly empty. The dream of a car for every scooter family slowly fades.

fired.title: The board takes the wheel
fired.text: After three costly calls, the board loses faith in you and hands the Nano project to someone else.

realHistory: The Nano was first shown in New Delhi on 10 January 2008 at ₹1 lakh, and the world called it the cheapest car. After protests over the land for its plant at Singur, West Bengal, Tata moved the plant to Sanand in Gujarat. In April 2009 over 2 lakh people booked it, and a draw picked the first 1,00,000 buyers. Prices rose twice in 2010, while the first buyers kept the old price. After a few cars caught fire, Tata offered free safety upgrades, but sales still fell to 509 in November 2010, and in December Tata gave every Nano a free four-year warranty. Its best year was about 75,000 cars, far below the 2.5 lakh plan. In 2013 Ratan Tata called the 'cheapest car' label a mistake, and production stopped in 2018.
